cards.front: Recall a key point about Procurement and Stock Management
cards.back: Procurement is the process of sourcing and purchasing materials: choosing reliable suppliers who offer the right quality, price, and delivery times.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Procurement and Stock Management
cards.back: Buffer stock is the minimum level of stock a business holds to prevent running out if demand unexpectedly increases or supply is delayed - a safety net.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Procurement and Stock Management
cards.back: Just-in-time (JIT) stock control means ordering stock to arrive only when needed: eliminates storage costs but requires reliable suppliers and accurate demand forecasting.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Procurement and Stock Management
cards.back: The bar gate stock control chart shows: maximum stock level, buffer stock level, re-order level (when to order), and lead time (time between ordering and delivery).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Procurement and Stock Management
cards.back: Technology in stock management: barcodes, RFID tags, and EPOS systems track stock in real time, trigger automatic re-ordering, and reduce human error.

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating stock control methods, use the SPR framework: Supplier reliability (can they deliver on time?), Predictability of demand (how stable is it?), Risk tolerance (can the business afford stockouts?). JIT works best with reliable suppliers and predictable demand.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Just-in-time stock management is always the best approach because it saves money on storage. Correct: JIT eliminates storage costs but increases risk: if a supplier is late, the business cannot fulfil orders, losing revenue and customer trust.
